# Genesis 1:1

Prepared for Sherman G. Laing · Quantum.Earth.Laing

Study assistance: GAUCIA, the designated assistant role in this conversation.

September 10, 2026

בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ

Consonantal Hebrew: בראשית ברא אלהים את השמים ואת הארץ

Transliteration: Bereshit bara Elohim et hashshamayim ve'et ha'aretz.

Genesis 1:1, KJV:

> In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.

| Hebrew word | Transliteration | Reading aid | Standard value |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: |
| בראשית | Bereshit | In the beginning | 913 |
| ברא | bara | created | 203 |
| אלהים | Elohim | God | 86 |
| את | et | Marks the definite direct object | 401 |
| השמים | hashshamayim | the heaven; the heavens | 395 |
| ואת | ve'et | and + direct-object marker | 407 |
| הארץ | ha'aretz | the earth | 296 |

The displayed consonantal text contains seven words and twenty-eight letters. Standard Hebrew gematria, with final letters taking their ordinary values and vowel marks excluded, gives 913 + 203 + 86 + 401 + 395 + 407 + 296 = 2,701. These are calculations on the displayed text. They are not additional words in the verse.

The New Testament witness begins with John 1:1–3, KJV:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
>
> The same was in the beginning with God.
>
> All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.

The Greek word translated “Word” in John 1:1 is λόγος, transliterated logos. Under standard Greek isopsephy, λ = 30, ο = 70, γ = 3, ο = 70, and ς = 200; therefore λόγος = 373. The accent does not contribute a numerical value. This selected word calculation accompanies the New Testament witness; it is not a calculation of the whole Greek verse.

In the preaching of this verse, we begin with thanksgiving. Father, open our understanding as we read Your Word. Give us reverence without fear of honest questions, conviction without pride, and patience to receive what You have actually said. Keep us from replacing Your testimony with our wishes. Teach us to recognize Your goodness in creation and Your grace in Jesus Christ. Let the knowledge we receive become obedience, and let our obedience become service to the people You place before us. We thank You for another day in which to listen, learn, and walk faithfully. In the Name of Jesus Christ, Amen.

“In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.” Before we hurry into the next verse, let this sentence establish our attention. Its subject is God. Its action is creation. Its scope is the heaven and the earth. The opening does not ask us first to admire ourselves or the sophistication of our explanations. It directs us to the One to Whom the created order owes its existence. This is why thanksgiving belongs at the doorway of the study. We approach a world we did not originate, a life we did not give ourselves, and a Word we are called to receive faithfully. The beginning of the account becomes the beginning of our posture: listening before claiming, receiving before possessing, and worshipping before congratulating ourselves.

Consider the first expression, Bereshit, rendered in the KJV as “In the beginning.” It places the creation account at its opening. The narrative brings us to the origin of the heaven and the earth, while God is already the acting subject. Genesis 1:1 does not narrate God's birth or describe His becoming God. We should notice that carefully. The beginning belongs to the creation being spoken of; the sentence presents God as its Creator. The broader scriptural witness will speak of His everlasting being. We do not need to press every later statement into the grammar of these first letters in order to receive the force of the opening. We can let the verse say what it says, then allow other Scripture to deepen our understanding.

There is a useful discipline here for reading the original language. Bereshit contains the prefixed Hebrew letter bet, functioning here as the preposition represented by “in,” attached to reshit, a word associated with beginning or firstness. Transliteration helps us follow the sound of the word; it is not a replacement for the Hebrew. Nor is an English phrase a separate Hebrew word for every English word we see. Translation moves meaning between languages with different structures. Our KJV reading remains “In the beginning.” Questions about the grammatical relationship between the opening verses can be studied carefully, but those questions should not make us pretend that a numerical value settles Hebrew syntax. The opening must be read as language before it is examined as a pattern.

When we hear “beginning,” we may immediately think about the beginnings in our own lives: a household, a vocation, a study, a difficult season, or a work we hope to complete. Such applications can be fruitful, but the verse first concerns God's creation of the heaven and the earth. Its meaning is greater than our personal projects. We gain a sound application by respecting that larger meaning. Because we live within God's creation, our beginnings also take place within a reality that depends upon Him. We can therefore begin our work with humility and prayer. We are not repeating the divine act of creation. We are receiving an opportunity to act faithfully with life, materials, understanding, and time that we did not bring into existence.

The next word is bara, “created.” In this verse, the Hebrew verb is a singular form with God as its subject. That gives the sentence a definite direction: God acts, and the heaven and the earth are the objects of His creative action. We should also distinguish the word's meaning from every doctrine associated with creation. Bara by itself is not a technical Hebrew phrase meaning “out of nothing.” The doctrine that creation ultimately depends on God, rather than on some independent eternal material, is considered through the wider witness of Scripture. Being careful about the verb does not weaken the verse. It helps us avoid making a dictionary entry say more than it does and helps us locate theological claims in the passages that actually support them.

There is wonder enough in the stated action. The sentence attributes the creation of the heaven and the earth to God. We do not have to manufacture additional meanings to make that declaration worthy of worship. Human beings can rearrange, cultivate, build, compose, discover, and invent. Those are meaningful activities, and later Scripture gives human work dignity and responsibility. But our activities take place within the created order. Our finest achievement does not make us the source of existence. This distinction protects both worship and work. It gives God the honor belonging to the Creator, and it allows us to value human workmanship without asking it to bear the weight of divinity. We can be grateful for an accomplishment while remembering the life and provision that made it possible.

The third word, Elohim, is translated “God.” Its form is plural in Hebrew, yet here it stands with the singular verb bara and refers to the one Creator acting in the sentence. We should not read the plural form as though Genesis 1:1 were announcing several gods cooperating. We should also avoid saying that the form of this noun, by itself, proves the full Christian doctrine of the Trinity. A Christian reading receives this verse together with the whole biblical witness, including what the New Testament says about the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The grammar is part of the evidence; it is not a substitute for the rest of Scripture. Careful observation and Christian confession can stand together without either being exaggerated.

Psalm 90:2 gives us a fitting witness to God's everlasting being: “Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.” This places our short lives before a greatness that does not depend on our span of years. We can become anxious because our time is limited, our strength changes, and our understanding develops slowly. The psalm invites us to consider God beyond those limits. In worship, that consideration becomes trust. We do not know every detail of the road ahead, but we can ask the everlasting God to establish our steps. His endurance is not a promise that every plan we devise will succeed. It is a reason to bring our plans before Him honestly.

The fourth word is et, written aleph-tav, את. In this sentence it serves as a marker of the definite direct object. It is part of Hebrew grammar and normally has no separate English word in the translation. Its presence helps mark what God created. Aleph and tav are the first and last letters of the Hebrew alphabet, a fact readers sometimes connect devotionally with biblical language about the first and the last. Such a connection must be named as a devotional association. The grammatical word et does not lexically mean Jesus, cross, covenant, or salvation. We do not need to assign it an unspoken translation in order to find the Son in the biblical account of creation. John explicitly supplies the Christian witness we need.

This is an occasion to practice reverence through restraint. A beautiful association can move the heart, but the movement of the heart does not automatically establish a translation. We honor Scripture when we distinguish what the text states, what another passage teaches, and what we are drawing as an illustration. That distinction does not prohibit meditation. It gives meditation a trustworthy foundation. If an illustration helps us remember a truth clearly taught elsewhere, we may receive it as an illustration. If it is presented as the hidden lexical meaning of a common grammatical particle, we should return to the language and reconsider. Faith does not require us to turn every interesting feature into a proof. It calls us to be faithful with the testimony we have received.

The fifth word, hashshamayim, is rendered “the heaven” in Genesis 1:1 in the KJV. The prefixed he supplies the definite article, “the.” The Hebrew noun shamayim has a plural-shaped ending and is conventionally rendered “heaven” or “heavens” according to context and translation. We should preserve the exact wording of the KJV quotation while acknowledging the form of the Hebrew. That is why the verse above says “the heaven,” even though the reading aid also gives “the heavens.” We are not correcting the quoted verse by silently replacing a word. We are distinguishing the chosen English translation from a note about the original language. Both can be visible, and each can serve its own purpose without being confused with the other.

The sixth word, ve'et, joins the conjunction represented by “and” to the direct-object marker. The seventh word, ha'aretz, means “the earth” in this verse. Together, “the heaven and the earth” expresses the comprehensive scope of the created order through the pairing of its great domains. The sentence is not merely interested in a small private space belonging to one family or people. Its horizon is the world in which all of us live. That broad horizon gives the opening a lasting moral weight. The earth cannot be treated as though its value began with our ownership or ended with our immediate use. It belongs within the work of God before it becomes the setting of our labor, habitation, conflict, or care.

Psalm 24:1 makes the connection plain: “The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein.” Ownership before God carries responsibility. We receive, use, tend, and pass on what lies within the creation. This can shape ordinary conduct: how we keep a home, how we speak to a neighbor, how we handle resources, and how we respond when something entrusted to us is damaged. Stewardship begins with the recognition that our power to use a thing is not the whole measure of what is right. A person can have ability without wisdom, access without care, or ambition without patience. Thanksgiving asks us to remember the Giver while considering what faithfulness requires of the recipient.

Now return to the numerical record. The twenty-eight letters are counted from the consonantal Hebrew shown above. Vowel points, accent marks, spaces, and punctuation are not counted as letters in this calculation. The seven word values use ordinary Hebrew letter values, including the ordinary values for final forms. Thus the final mem in Elohim and hashshamayim takes the value forty, and the final tsadi in ha'aretz takes the value ninety. The total of 2,701 belongs to this text under this declared convention. A different convention, spelling, or treatment of final letters could produce another result. Stating the method lets another reader repeat the arithmetic and understand why the result is what it is. Precision is a form of care for the person who comes after us.

The first word, Bereshit, gives bet two, resh two hundred, aleph one, shin three hundred, yod ten, and tav four hundred: 913. Bara gives two, two hundred, and one: 203. Elohim gives one, thirty, five, ten, and forty: 86. Et gives one and four hundred: 401. Hashshamayim gives five, three hundred, forty, ten, and forty: 395. Ve'et gives six, one, and four hundred: 407. Ha'aretz gives five, one, two hundred, and ninety: 296. Each value follows the displayed letters. We can therefore appreciate the order of the record while keeping our conclusions proportionate. Agreement in arithmetic establishes that the arithmetic agrees with the method; it does not, by itself, establish an interpretation of God's purposes.

The total also factors as 37 multiplied by 73. That is a true mathematical property of 2,701. What it signifies theologically is a separate question, and Genesis 1:1 does not provide an interpretation of those factors. We may notice a numerical relationship without claiming that it predicts an event, validates a personal identity, or reveals a command absent from the text. Scripture remains the governing witness. Numbers can help us inspect the form of a passage, just as counting words can help us describe it. They cannot assume the authority of a sentence God has not spoken. The appropriate response to an interesting pattern is careful attention, a reproducible calculation, and modesty about what has actually been shown.

This care is especially valuable when knowledge feels exciting. Discovery can awaken gratitude, but excitement can also tempt us to move too quickly from observation to certainty. The discipline of returning to the text makes room for correction. We can say, “This is the letter count,” “This is the calculation,” and “This is my proposed interpretation,” without blending those statements into one claim. A correction to our interpretation need not be treated as a failure of Scripture. It may be the fruit of listening more closely. Humility permits growth because it does not require every earlier conclusion to remain untouched. The Word we study deserves greater loyalty than the explanation we first offered about it. That loyalty can make our learning more peaceful as well as more truthful.

John 1:1 deliberately brings the Christian reader back to the language of beginning: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Notice the distinction between the creation that comes to be and the Word Who already “was.” John does not place the Word among the things later described as made through Him. He speaks of the Word in relation to God and identifies the Word as God. These are profound statements, and we should receive all their parts together. The Word was with God; the Word was God. The passage gives the Christian study of Genesis an explicit witness to the Word's presence at the beginning. We can rest the connection on John's words rather than on a hidden numerical equivalence.

John 1:2 continues, “The same was in the beginning with God.” Then verse three says, “All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.” The breadth of the statement matters. John speaks of all things made, and he repeats the point by excluding any made thing from independence of the Word. In the Christian reading, therefore, the Son is not introduced as a late addition to a universe that had no relation to Him. The created order owes its being to Him. The beginning in Genesis and the beginning in John are brought into conversation by Scripture itself. We can study each passage in its own wording and receive the witness they give together.

John 1:14 identifies the Word through the incarnation: “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.” Here the study moves toward the confession that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. The Word through Whom all things were made truly entered human life. Christianity does not leave the reader with an impersonal origin and no living relation to the Creator. John's testimony leads us to Jesus Christ. We should not weaken the incarnation into a metaphor for an idea becoming popular, nor turn it into a general title for every impressive human achievement. John is testifying concerning the One Whose glory the witnesses beheld.

That witness changes the tone of our meditation. The vastness of creation may make a person feel very small. John tells us that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. Divine greatness and the reality of the incarnation belong together in the Christian confession. We are not asked to choose between reverence for the Creator and attention to Jesus Christ. We learn to worship the Creator in the light of the Son made known in the Gospel. This also gives weight to truth and grace together. Truth calls us to honesty about what we know and how we live. Grace receives us as people who need mercy. A study of origins can therefore lead to repentance, gratitude, and trust, rather than ending as an exercise in abstraction.

The calculation of logos as 373 can remain in its appropriate place beside that testimony. It is an arithmetical description of a Greek word under a conventional system of letter values. It does not establish the identity of the Word; John supplies that testimony through sentences, relationships, and the unfolding account. Nor do unequal values between a Greek word and a Hebrew word separate passages that Scripture connects. Translation does not preserve every numerical property across alphabets. We therefore read the Greek word as part of John's language, recognize the declared calculation, and let the passage govern the theology. This approach allows exact data and reverent preaching to stand beside one another without asking either to perform the other's task.

Colossians 1:16 gives another New Testament witness: “For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him:” In its surrounding passage, Paul is speaking of the Son. The connection with Genesis is clear in the language of creation, heaven, and earth. Paul also speaks of purpose: all things were created “for him.” The Christian reader is therefore directed beyond origin alone. The created order is related to Christ in its purpose as well as in its coming to be. Our study must leave room for worship, because the passage concerns the One for Whom creation exists.

Colossians 1:17 continues, “And he is before all things, and by him all things consist.” The witness extends from creation to its continuing dependence on Christ. The verse does not supply a physics equation or identify a particular force measured by an instrument. It gives a theological confession about the relation of all things to Him. We should receive that confession in its own register. Scientific investigation can ask about processes and measurable relationships within creation. This passage speaks of creation's dependence upon Christ. Treating a theological sentence as though it were a laboratory result would confuse the kind of claim being made. Honoring the sentence means giving it its full theological force while remaining honest about the questions it does and does not directly answer.

Hebrews 11:3 also belongs beside Genesis 1:1: “Through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear.” The passage locates the believer's understanding within faith in God's creative command. It does not require us to imagine that what is invisible is unreal. It directs attention to God as the One Whose word accounts for what is seen. This is part of the wider biblical witness considered when Christians speak about creation's ultimate dependence upon God. We should preserve its wording and avoid turning it into a claim that a particular modern theory has been proved by the verse. Its stated concern is the understanding of faith.

Faith, in this setting, is not permission to label every uncertain idea a revelation. We trust the God to Whom the passage bears witness, and that trust should encourage honesty in the details of our study. If a proposed explanation lacks evidence, saying so can be an act of faithfulness. If a calculation contains an error, correcting it can serve the truth. If a question remains open, we need not conceal it to protect the authority of God. His authority does not depend on our appearing incapable of mistakes. The character of our study should reflect reverence for the One we confess. Careful work, patient inquiry, and willingness to learn can become expressions of gratitude for the understanding we have been given.

Acts 17:24–25 brings creation into the setting of public witness: “God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands; Neither is worshipped with men's hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things;” Paul presents God as the Giver of life and breath. God is not a dependent being maintained by human service. Worship recognizes His giving; it does not supply a lack in His existence. This is a needed correction to our tendency to imagine that our productivity makes us indispensable. We serve because we have received life, not because God must borrow life from us.

That testimony brings us back to the thanksgiving with which we began. Breath is so ordinary that we can pass through much of a day without considering it. Acts names it among God's gifts. Gratitude does not require an extraordinary result before it can begin. It can begin with life, with a chance to make amends, with a person to love, with food received, with a word of truth understood, or with strength sufficient for the next faithful action. None of this requires pretending that suffering is pleasant or that a difficult circumstance has already changed. Thanksgiving can speak truthfully from within an unfinished day. We acknowledge what has been given while also bringing before God what remains painful, uncertain, or beyond our present strength.

Revelation 4:11 gives creation the language of heavenly worship: “Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created.” The opening of Genesis and this scene of worship meet in the acknowledgment of the Creator. God is worthy. The verse directs glory and honor toward Him on the ground that He created all things. Our response, therefore, is more than curiosity about origins. Curiosity may begin the inquiry, but worship recognizes the worth of the One revealed. We can bring learning, questions, and gratitude into that recognition. Knowledge becomes rightly ordered when it serves truthful praise and faithful living rather than becoming an occasion for self-exaltation.

Notice also what this does to the way we speak about purpose. Colossians says creation is for Christ; Revelation places creation within the pleasure of God. Purpose is therefore not exhausted by our immediate success or disappointment. A day can contain faithful work without containing a dramatic achievement. A person can act with courage, honesty, and love even when a desired outcome remains distant. We should not use these passages to promise that every ambition will be fulfilled in the form we prefer. They invite us to place our ambitions before a purpose greater than our own. That can free us to ask better questions: whether our work is truthful, whether it serves our neighbor, and whether we are willing to receive correction along the way.

Genesis 1:1 also helps us preserve the distinction between the Creator and creation. The heaven and the earth are what God created. They are not presented as pieces of God that we can gather, measure, or assemble into His essence. We may study creation with great seriousness, including its mathematical regularities and the complexity of living things. The study can deepen our wonder. It does not make the object under examination identical with the God Who created it. Nor does a model of a natural process become a model containing the fullness of God. In worship, we acknowledge that distinction with gratitude. The world can bear witness to His work without becoming the object to which we give the worship belonging to Him.

Psalm 19:1 says, “The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.” Creation is presented as a witness to glory. A witness points beyond itself. When we admire a clear sky, the structure of a leaf, or the order we can describe in the natural world, thanksgiving can follow. Our admiration need not depend on inventing a secret message in every observation. The world is already worthy of attentive care as the work of God. This gives ordinary study a place within discipleship: looking closely, speaking accurately, and refusing to treat wonder as an excuse for carelessness. We can be moved by beauty while also being precise about the limits of the claims we make concerning it.

At the same time, Genesis 1:1 does not yet tell the whole biblical story. As we continue through Genesis, we will encounter humanity, command, disobedience, judgment, mercy, and promise. We must let those passages speak in their proper order. The opening establishes God as Creator; it does not make the later account of suffering and sin unnecessary. Christian hope rests within the fuller scriptural witness to redemption in Jesus Christ. We should therefore resist using the first verse to explain every painful event as though its particulars were transparent to us. We can confess the Creator while grieving honestly. We can give thanks while asking for help. We can trust God's faithfulness without claiming knowledge of purposes He has not disclosed to us.

There is a patient way to read this single verse aloud. Read the Hebrew as far as your present ability allows, then follow the transliteration without embarrassment about learning. Read the KJV slowly and let the sentence finish. Pause over its subject, its action, and its scope. Then read John 1:1–3 and John 1:14. Hear how the New Testament witness brings the Word and His incarnation into the study. Return once more to Genesis. This movement between passages is not a search for a concealed code. It is the ordinary work of allowing Scripture to bear witness alongside Scripture. Repetition can help attention settle, and settled attention can reveal how much we passed over when we first hurried through a familiar sentence.

We can also examine ourselves without turning the study into self-condemnation. Have we received today's life as a gift? Have we treated the people around us as obstacles to our plans, or as neighbors to whom we owe love? Have we said more than we know in order to appear certain? Have we allowed an unanswered question to become an excuse for neglecting a duty we already understand? These are applications drawn from the confession of the Creator and the wider biblical call to faithfulness. They are not additional translations of Genesis 1:1. Naming them as applications allows us to hear the call clearly while keeping the verse itself intact. We bring our lives before the Word and ask for wisdom to respond.

For the work entrusted to us, the beginning can become a practical rhythm of gratitude and care. We can establish what we have actually received, describe what we understand, and identify what still needs to be learned. We can preserve a sound result, correct a mistaken one, and acknowledge the people whose labor has helped us. We can refuse to give a spiritual title to an unverified claim merely because we desire it to be true. These habits do not diminish ambition; they give it a responsible shape. A faithful worker can aim high while remaining teachable. The glory belongs to God, and the task before us is to use our present opportunities with honesty, diligence, love, and proportionate judgment.

This is also a word of rest for the heart. We are responsible for faithfulness, but we are not the creators of heaven and earth. We can finish an honest day's portion without pretending that the whole world rests on our ability to keep every task moving. We can ask for help. We can allow another person to contribute. We can admit weariness and receive ordinary care. These are pastoral applications of creaturely dependence, developed in light of the wider biblical witness. They do not mean abandoning responsibility. They mean carrying responsibility as human beings before God. Gratitude can release us from the need to prove our worth through endless motion and return us to work that is purposeful, attentive, and bounded by real human needs.

As we stand at this first verse, let the central confession remain clear: God created the heaven and the earth. Let the New Testament witness remain beside it: all things were made through the Word, and the Word was made flesh. Let the calculations remain exact: seven words, twenty-eight consonantal letters, and a standard Hebrew total of 2,701. Let the interpretation remain accountable to the words from which it is drawn. And let our response become worship expressed in conduct. We have begun with thanksgiving because life is received before it is offered in service. We continue with attention because the Word deserves to be heard. We walk forward with humility because learning is still before us, and with hope because our trust is in God.

Let this confession also find a place at the family table and in the quiet moments of the day. A child can learn the first sentence of Genesis before understanding every question that adults bring to it. An older reader can return to that same sentence with deeper gratitude after years of difficulty and provision. We need not possess the same vocabulary to give thanks together. We can speak plainly of God's creative work, read the passage aloud, and ask how to care for what we have received. The study becomes part of a shared life when the truth we confess is accompanied by patience, kindness, and the willingness to listen to one another.

Heavenly Father, thank You for the heaven and the earth, for the life You have given, and for the testimony of Your Word. Thank You for Jesus Christ, the Word made flesh, full of grace and truth. Establish in us an honest love of Scripture. Where our understanding is small, teach us. Where our conclusions are mistaken, correct us. Where our hearts are troubled, grant us peace sufficient to remain faithful. Bless our household with love, patience, and a readiness to forgive. Guide the work of our hands so that what we do serves others and honors You. Let our study bear fruit in gratitude, obedience, and mercy. All glory and honor belong to You. In the Name of Jesus Christ, Amen.
